1	# Umbra — Track 2: Build with Graph Intelligence
2	
3	## What it decides
4	
5	Umbra turns an agent-authored change into an impact-aware code-review workflow:
6	it identifies changed definitions, follows their dependents through Entire
7	Graph, subtracts the code the checkpoint shows the agent examined, and ranks
8	the remaining shadow as review targets. It selects the tests that reach those
9	targets, runs them, and then runs a full-suite sweep to audit that selection.
10	
11	The decision is actionable: review the ranked `umbra` nodes first and run the
12	tests attached to them before accepting the change.
13	
14	## Graph evidence and verification
15	
16	Each report preserves the evidence behind its recommendation:
17	
18	- Changed definitions with source file and line span.
19	- Traversed graph relations, including callers, data-flow dependents, type
20	  consumers, imports, co-change files, and test reachability.
21	- Checkpoint-derived evidence of reads, edits, searches, and agent statements.
22	- Source locations, selected test identifiers, individual test results, and a
23	  full-suite leak check.
24	
25	The HTML report is a replayable eclipse map; `umbra.packet.md` is the concise
26	review handoff; `umbra.json` is the inspectable machine-readable record.
27	
28	## Run
29	
30	Requirements: the Entire CLI with Checkpoints enabled, the Entire Graph plugin,
31	Go, and the test runner for the target repository.
32	
33	```sh
34	go install github.com/u7k4rs6/Umbra/umbra/cmd/entire-umbra@main
35	entire umbra <checkpoint-id-or-commit> --test "pytest -v" --out ./umbra-out
36	open ./umbra-out/umbra.html
37	```
38	
39	For the included seeded fixture:
40	
41	```sh
42	cd umbra/fixtures/app && ./setup.sh && cd ../..
43	. umbra/fixtures/app/.venv/bin/activate
44	entire umbra 1c2cf29 --test "pytest -v" --out ./umbra-out
45	```
46	
47	## Evidence artifacts
48	
49	- `umbra/site/index.html` and `umbra/site/map.html`: static, inspectable demo.
50	- `umbra/site/sample/umbra.json`: seeded fixture report used by the demo.
51	- `umbra/site/self/umbra.html`: Umbra analyzing one of its own mapped commits.
52	- `umbra/fixtures/app`: source and tests for reproducing the seeded failure.
53	
54	## Limits
55	
56	Umbra is intentionally conservative: unavailable transcript evidence is shown
57	as `unknown`, not inferred. Graph relations that are unavailable or not
58	traversed are listed in the report. A selected-test pass is not treated as
59	proof; the full-suite sweep reports any missed failures as leaks.

95	## Where the documents turned out to be wrong
96	
97	Three corrections, all forced by real output rather than preference.
98	
99	1. **The checkpoint trailer is not hexadecimal.** ARCHITECTURE.md section 1
100	   describes `Entire-Checkpoint: <12 hex>`. The installed CLI writes a 26
101	   character ULID, for example `01M1PVD1WBK1J1J8GWDNJJR7XZ`. A hex-only pattern
102	   matched nothing and every commit fell through to the session-window
103	   fallback while reporting, wrongly, that the commit carried no trailer. The
104	   pattern now accepts alphanumeric ids of 6 to 40 characters, which covers the
105	   ULID, the 12 hex id of imported history and the 40 hex id of a carry-forward
106	   entry, and preserves case so `git log --grep` can match the exact text.
107	
108	2. **`pytest -q` cannot be verified.** PRD.md uses `pytest -q` in the command
109	   surface and in the 90-second demo. Quiet mode prints no per-test ids, so
110	   `graph verify` answers `output format not recognised` and records zero
111	   results. `pytest -v` parses cleanly. The default is now `pytest -v`, and the
112	   table says `add -v` when a baseline comes back exit-code only.
113	
114	3. **Flags after the reference were silently dropped.** The surface in PRD.md
115	   is `entire umbra <ref> [flags]`, but Go's flag package stops parsing at the
116	   first non-flag argument, so `entire umbra HEAD --run none` ignored
117	   `--run none` and failed asking for a test runner. Argv is now reordered
118	   before parsing, with boolean flags handled so they do not swallow the
119	   reference.
120	
121	Two smaller ones:
122	
123	- Entire has more than one wording for an absent summary. Imported checkpoints
124	  say `*No summary...*` and hook-written ones say `*Not generated yet...*`.
125	  Any fully italicised block is now treated as absent.
126	- `graph impact --format json` is better than the text shape the design
127	  sketched, because it carries `call_site.line` and `additional_sites`
128	  directly. It is now the primary path; the text parser is the fallback and is
129	  still tested.

174	The exposure comes from the checkpoint of the session that built Umbra, which
175	is one long session covering the whole build rather than a short session that

241	### Bugs the rendering found that reading would not have
242	
243	1. `html/template` treats the contents of any `<script>` element as JavaScript,
244	   so the embedded report was escaped into a string literal and the map drew
245	   nothing. It needs `template.JS`, not `template.HTML`.
246	2. Four sources each drew a 500px gradient and the overlap washed the middle of
247	   the map out, taking the labels with it. The share is scaled by the count.
248	3. Labels collided. The lower-scored one is hidden until interaction, and its
249	   disc is still drawn, so the map never claims a node does not exist.
250	4. In the day scheme the shadow mask made pools **brighter** than their
251	   surroundings, inverting the meaning on a light ground. Pools are painted with
252	   a token that is transparent at night and a soft dark by day.
253	5. At 360px the page scrolled sideways: the last replay tick sat on the edge and
254	   the reproduce command would not wrap.
255	6. Re-rendering appended a second set of replay ticks instead of replacing them.
256	7. `.replay button` outranked `.tick`, so every tick drew as a 40px button.

258	### What phase 11 found
259	
260	The semantic diff reported **no symbols at all** for `umbra/cmd`. The cause was
261	a `.gitignore` pattern I wrote in phase 0: an unanchored `entire-umbra`, meant
262	for the built binary, also matches the source directory `cmd/entire-umbra/`.
263	The whole command package was untracked for nine phases. Local tests passed the
264	entire time because the files were on disk. A fresh clone would not have built.
265	
266	This is the single most useful thing the build produced: a green test run is
267	not the same as a correct repository, and only a tool that looks at the
268	repository rather than the working tree could tell the difference.
269	
270	Running Umbra on its own build then found a limitation worth stating rather
271	than tuning away. On the commit where Umbra changed `shadow.Build`, all twelve
272	dependents came back umbra, including every scenario test. The reading is
273	correct: that change was made with a shell command rather than the editing
274	tool, so the session produced no read and no edit event for the file. **Umbra's
275	examined set is built from tool activity, so an agent that works through the
276	shell leaves no trace it can see.** It is in the README's limitations and in
277	`site/self/`.
278	
279	That self run also found two scrubber bugs:
280	
281	- Paths from outside the repository reached the timeline through search output.
282	  A path outside the repository can never match a symbol in the field, so it is
283	  noise, and carrying it out leaks the layout of the machine. Such paths are now

444	### Phase 13: the real four-hop leak chain
445	
446	**Path taken: the preferred one. The fixture gained the chain, and
447	ARCHITECTURE.md was left describing what it always described.**
448	
449	The design's `leak` scenario is a test four hops from the changed symbol,
450	reported as `path exists at depth 4 via render_lines`. The fixture had no such
451	chain, so the forensics had been tested at depth four against a graph built
452	inside the test. That proved the code path and proved nothing about the
453	fixture.
454	
455	`app/report.py` now holds `render_lines`, which calls `line_text`, which calls
456	`line_total`, which calls `compute_total`. `tests/test_report.py` reaches
457	`render_lines`. The hop count was measured before anything was asserted, using
458	the same path search the forensics use, against the re-captured snapshot:
459	
460	```
461	line_total           depth 1 via compute_total
462	line_text            depth 2 via line_total
463	render_lines         depth 3 via line_text
464	test_receipt_total   depth 4 via render_lines
465	```
466	
467	`entire graph impact` cannot show this on its own: it caps at `--depth 2`, so
468	it reports `line_total` and `line_text` and stops. The measurement had to come
469	from the field.
470	
471	Confirmed end to end rather than only in the scenario test. A throwaway commit
472	adding a fourth parameter to `compute_total`, with `app/report.py` left
473	unchanged, produces:
474	
475	```
476	probes  8 selected  0 cracked
477	        1 further test(s) failed that no probe covered; they are listed as leaks below
478	sweep   full suite  1 leak
479	        tests/test_report.py::test_receipt_total  path exists at depth 4 via render_lines
480	```
481	
482	That is the string in the JSON example in ARCHITECTURE.md section 7, produced
483	by a real run rather than written into a fixture.
484	
485	**What it perturbed, which was little.** The scenarios read a captured snapshot
486	rather than the live fixture, so re-capturing it was the only way the new chain
487	could reach them. Exactly one scenario broke: `everything-lit` asserts nothing
488	is in shadow, and the two new symbols in `app/report.py` were unread. Its
489	transcript gained a read of that module and of the new test file, which is what
490	the scenario means. No other scenario's assertions moved. One unit test
491	asserted `compute_total` starts at line 20; the fixture had grown by then, so
492	that assertion is now structural rather than a line number, which is what it
493	was really testing.

495	**A reporting bug the new scenario exposed.** With a leak that actually fails,
496	the terminal read `probes 8 selected 1 cracked` and then named a test that was
497	not among the eight. The sweep's failures were being folded into the same list
498	as the probes' failures. A test the sweep turns up is a leak by definition, so
499	cracked now counts only probes that were selected and failed, and a failure no

504	### Phase 13: what the end to end tests found by failing in a clone
505	
506	The exit-code tests passed here and failed the moment they ran in a fresh
507	clone. That is the phase 11 lesson again, and this time it surfaced two product
508	bugs and one piece of fragility in the test itself.
509	
510	**1. `graph checkpoint` was answering about the wrong commit.** `LoadSources`
511	tries `graph checkpoint <id>` first, because ARCHITECTURE.md calls it the
512	documented bridge between Graph and Checkpoints. But it returns the changes of
513	the commit *that checkpoint belongs to*. When a reference is paired with a
514	checkpoint by session window, that is a guess about which session produced the
515	commit and says nothing about which commit the checkpoint owns. In this working
516	copy the pairing happens to choose an imported checkpoint, which has no commit,
517	so the fallback runs and the report is correct. In a clone it chose a
518	hook-written checkpoint that does own a commit, and the report described that
519	commit's changes under the header of the one the reader asked for: the header
520	said `1c2cf29` while the sources were the transcript package from phase 3. The
521	bridge is now used only when the reference resolved through the trailer or
522	through the checkpoint id, where the two are the same piece of work.
523	
524	**2. A stale worktree poisoned every later run.** Worktrees are keyed by commit
525	under a shared data directory, so two checkouts of one repository, or a run
526	that died before its cleanup, collide on the same path. The code reused
527	anything with a `.git` in it. A worktree left behind by a checkout that had
528	since been deleted made git unable to read its metadata and Graph refuse to run
529	there, for every subsequent run against that commit from any checkout. A
530	leftover is now reused only when it is a healthy checkout sitting at the wanted
531	commit, and otherwise removed and pruned first.
532	
533	**3. The tests were asserting on states that are not repository state.** They
534	checked that a given commit has umbra nodes. Node states come from the examined
535	set, which comes from whichever checkpoint the reference pairs with, and the
536	set of checkpoints present differs between a working copy and a clone: imported
537	history is local and is not pushed. The same commit reports six umbra nodes
538	here and none in a clone, both correct. The tests now run the binary once,
539	read the summary from its JSON, and derive a condition that must fire from what
540	the report actually says. They also skip when the toolchain cannot analyse the
541	checkout at all, which happens where Graph refuses to run git, the same
542	restriction phase 12 hit when recording from a temporary directory.
543	
544	Verified in three places before the commit: this working copy, a clone under
545	`$HOME`, and a clone under the restricted scratch directory, where the suite
546	skips cleanly rather than failing.

625	## Phase 15: the scrubber becomes the only exit
626	
627	Five scrubbing bugs so far have been the same bug five times: an output path
628	that wrote without going through the scrubber. Each was fixed where it was
629	found, which fixed that path and left the shape intact.
630	
631	| # | Phase | The path that wrote unscrubbed |
632	|---|---|---|
633	| 1 | 11 | Paths from outside the repository reached the timeline through search output |
634	| 2 | 11 | The base64 heuristic redacted git object ids and worktree paths, so the reproduce list could not be checked |
635	| 3 | 12 | The recording carried an email address; the scrubber had no rule for one |
636	| 4 | 14.1 | `graph.Verify` appended its commands to `a.Commands` raw, bypassing the scrubber every other command went through |
637	| 5 | 14.2 | Only `umbra record` set `scrub.Names`, so an ordinary run left the author's display name in the timeline |
638	
639	Number 2 is the odd one out: it removed too much rather than too little. The
640	other four are the same shape.
641	
642	### The inventory, before anything changed
643	
644	Every place an artifact is written, and whether it scrubbed:
645	
646	| Writer | What it writes | Scrubbed before phase 15 |
647	|---|---|---|
648	| `emit` stdout, `--format table` | terminal table | only whatever the builder happened to scrub |
649	| `emit` stdout, `--format json` | report JSON | same |
650	| `emit` stdout, `--format packet` | packet markdown | same |
651	| `emit --out`, `umbra.json` | report JSON | same |
652	| `emit --out`, `umbra.packet.md` | packet markdown | same |
653	| `emit --out`, `umbra.html` | map, with the JSON embedded | same |
654	| `report.BuildLayout` via `emit` | node and ring label text inside the map | **no**, it ran before any scrub and copied node names into the layout |
655	| `runner.Recorder.Save` | `fixtures/recorded/*/recording.json` | yes, but through a nil-able function, and `--no-scrub` turned it off |
656	| `gen-site` | `site/umbra.css`, `site/umbra.js` | not applicable, they are source assets |
657	| `gen-site` `embedSample` | the JSON embedded in `site/index.html` | **no check of its own**, it inherited whatever the committed sample carried |
658	| `analyze.go` | the reproduce list | yes, since 14.1 |
659	| `execute.go` | the verify commands in the reproduce list | yes, since 14.1 |
660	
661	"Only whatever the builder happened to scrub" is the honest description of the
662	old state. Values were scrubbed as they were built, one call site at a time,
663	and the renderers took an `*Analysis` and wrote whatever was in it. Nothing in
664	the type system knew the difference between an analysis that had been through
665	the scrubber and one that had not.
666	
667	### The choke point
668	
669	`report.Sealed` wraps an `*Analysis` in an unexported field. `report.Seal` is
670	the only way to make one, and `WriteJSON`, `MarshalJSON`, `HTML`, `Packet` and
671	`Table` all take a `Sealed` and refuse a zero value. `BuildJSON` is now
672	`buildJSON` and unexported. A new output path cannot skip the scrubber by
673	omission, because there is nothing for it to write from until it has sealed
674	something.
675	
676	`Seal` scrubs every string in the analysis that could carry text from the
677	machine, then builds the layout from the scrubbed values. That ordering is the
678	fix for the row marked no above: the layout carries node names and file names
679	as label text, and building it first meant a scrubbed report could ship with an
680	unscrubbed picture on it. Nothing had leaked that way yet. It was open.
681	
682	A nil scrubber means the default one for this machine, never no scrubbing.
683	There is no flag for less. `umbra record --no-scrub` is gone: a recording is
684	committed, and a flag that turns off scrubbing on a committed artifact is the
685	next bug in the table above waiting for someone to forget it.
686	
687	### One derivation of the scrub inputs
688	
689	`Options.Scrubber` derives home, repository, user, host and the git author
690	names once and caches them on the options. `umbra record` and the analysis
691	pipeline both call it and get the same value. Bug 5 was possible only because
692	there were two constructions and one of them was missing a line.
693	
694	### The output-wide check
695	
696	`report.ScanArtifact` reads finished bytes and reports absolute home paths,
697	addresses, token shapes and supplied display names, with line numbers. It does
698	not care which code path produced the bytes, which is the point: a new writer
699	is covered the day it exists rather than the day someone adds it to a list.
700	
701	`TestNoGeneratedArtifactCarriesAnythingPrivate` walks `site/`,
702	`fixtures/recorded/` and `docs/renders/` rather than naming files, and takes
703	the author names from `git log` so it fails for whoever cloned the repository
704	as readily as for its author. **It scans 25 artifacts and found nothing.** The
705	existing corpus needed no re-scrubbing, and the self report regenerated through
706	the sealed pipeline is byte-identical to the committed one.
707	
708	`gen-site` now runs the same scan before embedding either sample, so a report
709	produced by an older build or edited by hand cannot reach the landing page.

711	## Phase 15: a known-positive for every check
712	
713	Four verifications in this project have returned a confident pass that was
714	wrong: the `.gitignore` case where the local tests were green but a clone would
715	not build, the cracked-probe count that named a test outside the selection, the
716	commit check that counted `ok` lines instead of looking for `FAIL`, and the
717	refs audit that reported thirty refs of zero bytes because `git ls-tree` is
718	scoped to the working directory. Every one of them had only ever passed. A
719	check that has never been observed to fail is not a check yet.
720	
721	Each of these plants what the check is for and asserts it says so. All the
722	planted values are invented: `plantedperson` is not a user on any machine and
723	`example.invalid` is reserved by RFC 2606, so the address can never be real.
724	
725	| Test | Planted | Mutation that proved it fires |
726	|---|---|---|
727	| `TestScannerCatchesPlantedHomePathEmailAndAuthorName` | a home path, an address, an author name | removed the address pattern; the scanner missed the address |
728	| `TestSealRemovesWhatTheScannerFinds` | the same three, into the analysis | stopped sealing `a.Commands`; the home path reached line 262 of the JSON |
729	| `TestRenderersRefuseAnUnsealedAnalysis` | a zero `Sealed` | none needed; it asserts an error each renderer only returns for the unsealed case |
730	| `TestCrackedProbesNeverCountsAFailureOutsideTheSelection` | a failure the selection never ran | made `CrackedProbes` return `NewFailures`; the leak was counted as a crack |
731	| `TestParseVerdictCatchesAPlantedFailure` | a run reporting `NEWLY FAILING` | broke the pattern; newly failing came back empty |
732	| `TestParseVerdictDoesNotMiscountTheWordOk` | passing lines with `ok` in the test names | the negative half of the same pair |
733	| `TestCheckSampleIsRealCatchesAPlantedFabrication` | `sample000class`, an all-zero commit, no commit | disabled the prefix check; the invented id was accepted |
734	| `TestCheckSampleIsCleanCatchesAPlantedAddress` | an address in a report about to be published | shares the scanner's mutation above |
735	| `TestAuditCatchesPlantedEmail` | a checkpoint ref whose transcript carries both | see below |

770	## Phase 16: the eclipse hero
771	
772	The landing page is restyled around a drawn total eclipse. Nothing in the
773	report, the report template, the drop-in viewer's behaviour or any Go file
774	changed. The new files are `site/landing.css`, `site/corona.js` and a rewritten
775	`site/index.html` and `site/site.js`. `site/umbra.css` and `site/umbra.js` are
776	still the report's own, copied by `gen-site`, and still byte-identical to it.
777	
778	### The corona is a renderer
779	
780	There is no raster asset on the page and no request for one. `corona.js` builds
781	the eclipse in inline SVG: layered radial gradients warped by a `feTurbulence`
782	`fractalNoise` with a fixed seed through an `feDisplacementMap`, streamers laid
783	along the x axis and rotated to their angles, an occluding disc taken out by a
784	mask, a bright ring hugging the limb, and one bright limb point with an
785	anisotropic flare made from a rotated linear gradient and one blur.
786	
787	It is deterministic. Nothing calls `Math.random`. The limb angle comes from a
788	hash of the checkpoint's commit and the streamer geometry from a small linear
789	generator seeded by the same number, so the same `umbra.json` always draws the
790	same corona. The filament count reads the report: twenty, plus forty six times
791	the lit fraction, plus three per source. More of the field in the light means a
792	denser corona, and the number comes from `summary`, not from a constant chosen
793	because it looked good.
794	
795	Cost was a real constraint, not a note. Every filter has an explicit
796	`filterUnits="userSpaceOnUse"` region, so it rasterises once at a fixed size.
797	No filter primitive is ever animated. The only thing that moves after the first
798	paint is a clip inset and an opacity. The day layer is a second copy of the
799	same two SVGs, so it would rasterise the turbulence twice; it is therefore
800	built only when the divider is off its resting position, which means an
801	ordinary visit pays for one corona.
802	
803	Four attempts, each judged from a screenshot rather than from the code:
804	
805	1. Uniform thick filaments over a strong body read as a cartoon sunburst, and
806	   the brightest part of the gradient sat *inside* the moon where nothing could
807	   see it.
808	2. Peaking the gradient at the limb fixed that and produced a visible circular
809	   rim at the outer edge.
810	3. Softening the tail moved the rim but did not remove it. The cause was that
811	   the outer stops were written as multiples of the limb radius, so the last
812	   one fell past the end of the gradient and the alpha dropped from 0.012 to
813	   zero inside the final one percent of the radius. Writing the tail in
814	   absolute fractions removed it.
815	4. The limb flare was drawn on top of the moon and read as a scratch across the
816	   disc. It is now drawn behind the moon, with only the bead in front, which is
817	   also what actually happens.
818	
819	### The hero is the live map wearing the eclipse
820	
821	The map is the same `renderInto` from `umbra.js`, drawn from the layout already
822	in `umbra.json`. The JS still computes no positions. The occluding disc sits at
823	the layout centre, so the four changed symbols are inside it and their
824	dependents sit in the corona at ring radii the Go code chose.
825	
826	One thing had to give. The map paints its own background rectangle in
827	`--night`, as the spec requires, and that rectangle covered the corona behind
828	it. The rectangle is made transparent by a CSS rule on the landing page and the
829	stage carries the ground colour instead. `umbra.js` is untouched; a CSS `fill`
830	outranks the presentation attribute it sets.

832	### The four beats
833	
834	`01 CLAIM`, `02 FIELD`, `03 THE CUT`, `04 SWEEP`, in the project's own words.
835	Each drives the map to a real point in the timeline: seq 0, the last event
836	before the cut, `t0` itself, and the end. The page loads at `04`, which is the
837	eclipse, so nothing moves before first paint.

843	### Day and night
844	
845	The divider is a real inversion, not a filter. The day side is a second drawing
846	of the same two SVGs under day tokens, clipped by `clip-path`, so its gradients
847	and pools are computed from day values and the shadow pools stay darker than
848	the paper around them. Cloning needed one thing that is easy to miss: duplicate
849	ids in one document resolve to whichever came first, so the day copy would have
850	pointed at the night layer's gradients and inherited the night palette. Every
851	id in the copy is suffixed.

853	It is a `role="slider"`, operable with the arrow keys, and it settles to
854	whichever scheme it was left nearest. `Home`, `End` and `Space` are stopped at

913	### Ground colour, measured rather than argued
914	
915	The hero rendered twice at the same viewport and the same playhead, once on the
916	current pure black and once on FRONTEND_SPEC.md's `#10141C`:
917	`docs/renders/ground-black.png` and `docs/renders/ground-nearblack.png`.
918	
919	Sampling the luminance along the horizontal from the eclipse centre outwards,
920	the corona's geometry is identical in both, reaching the ground at the same
921	+372px. What differs is whether the tail can be seen getting there.
922	
923	| Distance from the limb | On black | On `#10141C` |
924	|---|---|---|
925	| ground level | 0.00 | 19.73 |
926	| +60px | 14.05 above ground, rgb 20,13,7 | 11.98 above ground, rgb 34,31,32 |
927	| +120px | 32.17 above ground | 28.31 above ground, rgb 60,46,33 |
928	| +200px | 2.49 above ground | 1.49 above ground, rgb 20,21,27 |
929	| +280px and beyond | 0.00 | 0.00 |
930	
931	Two things go wrong on the lifted ground. The tail is clamped: from +200px out
932	it sits within 1.5 luminance units of the ground, so the last 170px of corona
933	is in the pixels but not in the eye, and the light reads as stopping at +200px
934	rather than fading to nothing. And the warm tail desaturates: at +60px it
935	renders rgb 34,31,32, which is neutral grey, because a low-alpha warm layer
936	summed with a blue-black ground lands off the warm axis. At +200px the blue
937	channel is actually **lower** than the ground's own, so the faintest corona is
938	a cool smudge rather than warm light.
939	
940	**Pure black holds the corona better**, and the reason is specific to this
941	page: the corona is the light source here, and a light field is only as long as
942	the floor it falls to. The spec's argument for the blue-black is that a neutral
943	near-black with one neon accent reads as a template, and that argument is
944	answered by the full warm ramp rather than by lifting the floor. Not changed.

970	
971	The landing page was asked to feel like designcode.io: dynamic, interactive,
972	alive. The site was opened in Playwright and read rather than recalled, and
973	what was taken from it is the interaction vocabulary, not the surface.
974	
975	What it is actually made of, from its own computed styles: Inter and Geist
976	Sans, a near-black `#020202` ground, a blue and violet gradient beam, rounded
977	glass cards, and one easing everywhere,
978	`cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1)`, on transitions like
979	`opacity 1s, transform 1s, filter 0.9s`. That last line is the whole trick: a
980	blur-and-rise reveal on an expo-out curve.
981	
982	**Taken:** the blur reveal and its easing, a persistent hairline grid, a sticky
983	bar that condenses on scroll, a section rail that tracks where you are, a

987	**Refused:** its fonts and its colours, which is what the brief said was wrong
988	with it. Inter and Geist are the default of every developer landing page
989	shipped this year, and the blue-violet gradient is the same. The page keeps its
990	own single warm hue and gains a stronger type position rather than a borrowed
991	one.

994	
995	The body was a UI sans inherited from the report's stylesheet. It is now the
996	serif, the same one the display uses. Two families carry the whole page: the
997	serif for anything a person reads in sentences, the monospace for anything the

| `pallets/flask` | BSD-3-Clause | ~7k (`src/flask`) | ~7k | ~8s | Fine size, but a large share of Flask's behaviour delegates to Werkzeug, which is out of repo. Umbra only traverses in-repo edges, so the blast radius would be artificially thin and I would be testing the wrong thing. |
| `Textualize/rich` | MIT | ~32k | ~13k | ~25s | In range but at the top of it, and many modules are leaf renderables with few internal callers. Slower suite, shallower graph. |

result.output:
`HelpFormatter.write_usage` breaks options at a hyphen

If an option containing a hyphen in its name is printed at the line break limit, it’s broken at the hyphen.

### Reproduction

```python
import click

options = [
    "--enable-verbose-logging",
    "--output-file-path",
    "--max-retry-count",
    "--disable-cache-mode",
    "--config-file-location",
    "--user-auth-token",
    "--auto-update-interval",
    "--force-overwrite-existing",
    "--network-timeout-seconds",
    "--debug-trace-enabled",
]

f = click.HelpFormatter(width=65)
f.write_usage("program", " ".join(options))
print(f.getvalue())
```

### Expected output
```
Usage: program --enable-verbose-logging --output-file-path
               --max-retry-count --disable-cache-mode
               --config-file-location --user-auth-token
               --auto-update-interval --force-overwrite-existing
               --network-timeout-seconds --debug-trace-enabled
```

### Actual output
```
Usage: program --enable-verbose-logging --output-file-path --max-
               retry-count --disable-cache-mode --config-file-
               location --user-auth-token --auto-update-interval
               --force-overwrite-existing --network-timeout-
               seconds --debug-trace-enabled
```

### Environment

- Python version: 3.12.3
- Click version: 8.3.1

### Additional information

#### `width` option

This also happens without specifying `width`. The `width` option is altered in the example to make the issue more frequent.

#### Relevance to other use cases

This may likely only affect:

- direct users of `click.HelpFormatter`,
- users of `click.argument` with custom `metavar` containing hyphens. 

On the other hand, `click` prints `[OPTIONS]` instead of listing individual options on the usage line and uses underscores instead of hyphens in argument names (unless specifying `metavar`).

#### Cause

I looked into the code and found that `textwrap.TextWrapper` is used under the hood, which has the [`break_on_hyphens`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/textwrap.html#textwrap.TextWrapper.break_on_hyphens) option. However, there is no option for the `click` user to influence this, apart from reimplementing `HelpFormatter.write_usage` (in a subclass) and `wrap_text`.

def test_write_usage_does_not_break_options_at_a_hyphen():
    """Issue #3362: ``HelpFormatter.write_usage`` wrapped hyphenated option
    names mid-token, because ``textwrap`` breaks on hyphens by default.
    """
    options = [
        "--enable-verbose-logging",
        "--output-file-path",
        "--max-retry-count",
        "--disable-cache-mode",
        "--config-file-location",
        "--user-auth-token",
        "--auto-update-interval",
        "--force-overwrite-existing",
        "--network-timeout-seconds",
        "--debug-trace-enabled",
    ]
    f = click.HelpFormatter(width=65)
    f.write_usage("program", " ".join(options))
    assert f.getvalue() == (
        "Usage: program --enable-verbose-logging --output-file-path\n"
        "               --max-retry-count --disable-cache-mode\n"
        "               --config-file-location --user-auth-token\n"
        "               --auto-update-interval --force-overwrite-existing\n"
        "               --network-timeout-seconds --debug-trace-enabled\n"
    )


def test_write_usage_long_prefix_does_not_break_at_a_hyphen():
    """The branch that puts the arguments on their own line keeps
    hyphenated tokens whole too.
    """
    f = click.HelpFormatter(width=30)
    f.write_usage("a-very-long-program-name", "--max-retry-count --output-file-path")
    for line in f.getvalue().splitlines():
        assert not line.endswith("-")


def test_wrap_text_break_on_hyphens():
    """``wrap_text`` breaks on hyphens by default and stops when asked."""
    text = "alpha --max-retry-count"
    assert click.formatting.wrap_text(text, width=14) == "alpha --max-\nretry-count"
    assert (
        click.formatting.wrap_text(text, width=14, break_on_hyphens=False)
        == "alpha\n--max-retry-count"
    )
EOF

# Umbra on a repository that is not our fixture

**Umbra performed badly.** It ran without crashing, it was fast, and its
report was internally consistent, but on `pallets/click` it never traversed
the dependents of the method the session actually changed, it selected one
probe out of 2,059 tests, and when a planted mutation broke 51 tests its
full-suite sweep reported **zero leaks**. The sweep is the mechanism the
README calls "a selection that audits itself", and it failed silently in
exactly the case it exists for. Three of the five failures below are
invisible on `fixtures/app` for structural reasons: the fixture changes only
module-level functions, its blast radius is two hops from a test, and it never
breaks more than five tests at a time. The ranking, judged node by node, was
better than the plumbing: one of the top five was right, one defensible, and
three were wrong, and the one node whose behaviour actually changed was ranked
third.

Nothing in this document was fixed. This is a finding, not a patch.

---

## 1. The target

| | |
|---|---|
| Repository | `pallets/click`, https://github.com/pallets/click |
| License | BSD-3-Clause |
| Base commit | `6aabf099bfdd4c1e75fe8d0e0d4241372b988ab1` ("Stable (#3851)") |
| Analysed commit | `562e458efd9de02e0f0e398381178c794c10990f` |
| Source | 12,727 lines of Python across 17 files under `src/` |
| Tests | 15,240 lines across 58 files under `tests/` |
| Parsed by Graph | 158 files, of which 90 are Python |

### The candidates, before anything was cloned

Sizes and licenses came from the GitHub API. Line counts and suite runtimes
were estimates from prior knowledge at proposal time and were replaced with
measurements after the pick was cloned.

| Candidate | License | Est. source lines | Est. suite | Judgement |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `pallets/click` | BSD-3-Clause | ~9.5k | ~5s, no network | Picked |
| `pallets/flask` | BSD-3-Clause | ~7k | ~8s | Right size, but much of Flask's behaviour delegates to Werkzeug, which is out of repo. Umbra only traverses in-repo edges, so the blast radius would have been thin for a reason that has nothing to do with Umbra |
| `Textualize/rich` | MIT | ~32k | ~25s | At the top of the range, and many modules are leaf renderables with few internal callers. Slower suite, shallower graph |

Click was picked because the property under test, a changed symbol having
several genuine in-repo dependents at depth 1 and 2 with tests among them, is
a property of click's own structure rather than something a fixture author
arranged. Its suite is also fast enough that probe selection has to earn its
keep. The estimate of ~9.5k source lines was low: the real figure is 12,727.

## 2. Setup, and the baseline

Cloned under `$HOME` because Graph refuses git subprocesses under paths it
considers unsafe, which the build notes already record. A venv with
`pip install -e . pytest`. `entire enable --agent claude-code`, then
`entire configure --skip-push-sessions`, and the origin push URL was set to a
non-existent value so nothing from this experiment could ever reach
`pallets/click`.

Baseline on a clean checkout, three consecutive runs:

```
2059 passed, 24 skipped, 31000 deselected, 1 xfailed in 3.36s   wall 4.02
2059 passed, 24 skipped, 31000 deselected, 1 xfailed in 2.85s   wall 3.45
2059 passed, 24 skipped, 31000 deselected, 1 xfailed in 2.82s   wall 3.42
```

The 31,000 deselected tests are click's `stress` marker, excluded by its own
`addopts`. **A 3 second suite changes what probe selection is worth.** On this
repository a reviewer can simply run everything, and the only thing selection
buys is a named list of which tests to look at first. That is worth saying
plainly before any of the numbers below: the strongest argument for probe
selection does not apply here.

### One environment problem worth recording

`pip install -e .` under flit writes a `click.pth` containing the absolute
path of the original checkout. Umbra runs tests in a **detached worktree**, so
`import click` inside that worktree resolves back to the working tree, not to
the commit under analysis. Both the baseline run and the head run would have
imported the same source, and `verify` would have found no difference no
matter what the commit did.

This was worked around, not fixed: a wrapper on `PATH` that puts `$PWD/src`
at the front of `PYTHONPATH` before invoking pytest, which wins over a `.pth`
entry. It was verified to work by planting mutations and watching them show up.

The general shape is worth naming: **Umbra's worktree isolation is real for
git and imaginary for an interpreted language installed in editable mode.**
Every Python project in the world develops this way. Nothing in the report
tells the reader whether isolation actually held.

## 3. The session

Nested `claude` invocations are blocked in this environment, so the session
could not be produced by a separate headless agent run inside the click repo.
The work was done from this session instead, and the session's own Claude Code
transcript was imported into the click repository with
`entire import claude-code --path`, unmodified. No part of the transcript was
edited or removed. Three checkpoints were created, one per user turn, and
Umbra paired the commit with the last of them, `65ddfb5e3bd3`, by session
window.

**The work.** Click issue #3362: `HelpFormatter.write_usage` breaks hyphenated
option names across a line, because `textwrap.TextWrapper` has
`break_on_hyphens=True` by default and click gives no way to change it. The
issue was chosen from click's open issue list before anything was read, on the
grounds that it was a genuine bug with a clear cause, not because of what it
would do to a graph.

The fix: `wrap_text` gained a `break_on_hyphens: bool = True` parameter passed
through to the `TextWrapper` constructor, and both `wrap_text` calls inside
`HelpFormatter.write_usage` pass `False`. Three regression tests were appended
to `tests/test_formatting.py` and a `CHANGES.md` entry added. The full suite
was run (2,062 passed) and the change committed.

**How the work was done, which turns out to matter more than what it was.**
The bug was reproduced with an inline `python -c`. `src/click/_textwrap.py`
and `src/click/formatting.py` were read in full with the file tool.
`tests/test_formatting.py` was read with an offset, lines 505 to 604. Four
edits to `formatting.py` went through the edit tool. The tests were appended
with a shell heredoc and `CHANGES.md` was patched with an inline Python
script, both through Bash. Everything else, greps, test runs, the commit, was
Bash.

Umbra's own coverage line describes this accurately:

```
coverage  3 file reads, 4 edits, 0 searches, 43 shell commands
```

Three reads and forty-three shell commands. This session is a textbook case of
the limitation the README already documents, and it is not an unusual session.

## 4. The run

```
entire umbra 562e458 --test "click-pytest -v" --out ./out
```

### Field size and timings

| | |
|---|---|
| Snapshot | 158 files parsed, **3,310 symbols, 9,582 relations**, completeness `ok` |
| Relations by kind | CALLS 2,706, DEFINES 3,310, CONTAINS 1,070, IMPORTS 607, USES_TYPE 271, CONSTRUCTS 266, DATA_FLOWS 264, SIMILAR_TO 236, INHERITS 117, PARAM_TYPE 98, OVERRIDES 86, **TESTS 18** |
| `graph snapshot`, cold | **2.92s** |
| `graph snapshot`, warm | 0.10s to 0.14s |
| `graph commit --json` | 0.17s |
| `graph impact --format json` | **3.11s and 3.14s** per call, five calls in this run |
| Whole run, wall clock | **28s** |

The impact calls are the run. Each one reports `index_latency_ms: 2911` and
`query_latency_ms: 1`: the index is rebuilt per invocation and the query
itself is free. Five sources means five rebuilds of the same index, roughly
15.5 of the 28 seconds. Everything else, the two worktrees, the snapshot, the
commit diff, the transcript parse, the probe pair and the full sweep pair,
fits in the remaining 12.5 seconds, and the sweep pair alone is about 7 of
those because the suite runs twice.

### The state breakdown and the coverage line

```
light  ●●●◐◐◐◐◐◐◐◐◐◐◐◐○   3 lit  12 penumbra  1 umbra  0 unknown   19% examined
coverage  3 file reads, 4 edits, 0 searches, 43 shell commands
```

Sixteen nodes. Thirteen in shadow. On a repository of 3,310 symbols, a change
to the help formatter produced a field of sixteen.

The three lit nodes are `HelpFormatter.write_dl`, `write_text` and
`write_usage`, all in `formatting.py`, which was read in full. Correct.

### Probes, cracks and the sweep

```
probes  1 selected  0 cracked
sweep   full suite  0 leaks
verdict NO EFFECT, the target tests behave exactly as before your edit
```

One probe, `tests/test_formatting.py::test_wrap_text_visible_width`, out of
2,059 tests. The sweep's zero leaks is correct **for this commit**: the change
genuinely alters no existing assertion. Section 6 shows what the same sweep
does when the change is not benign.

### Evidence tiers

Umbra's own tiers, on the thirteen shadowed nodes: **1 glance, 11 echo,
1 umbra, 0 unknown**, plus 3 lit.

The eleven echoes are the finding in this section, and section 5 returns to
them.

Relation mix: **4 direct caller, 12 type consumer**. No data flow, no
transitive caller, no co-change, no import. On the fixture almost every node
is a direct caller. Here three quarters of the field arrived over
`PARAM_TYPE`, `USES_TYPE` and `RETURNS_TYPE` edges, which say "this function
takes a `HelpFormatter`", not "this function calls the thing you changed".

**On "how many dependents came back heuristic or needing verification": none,
because this Graph build does not offer that.** `entire graph impact
--format json` in `v0.4.1-nightly.202609030616.ddcebd05` returns endpoints
with `relation`, `direction` and `depth`, and carries no `evidence`,
`confidence` or `verified` field anywhere in the document. There is no tier
for Umbra to report and none is reported. Any expectation of a heuristic
versus verified split in the output was an expectation about a Graph that does
not exist yet.

## 5. Judging the top five as a reviewer

For context, what a reviewer should actually worry about: `write_usage` now
wraps every usage line differently, which reaches every `--help` screen and
every parameter error in every program built on click, and `wrap_text` gained
a keyword parameter that no existing caller passes.

### 1. `CustomFormatter`, `tests/test_custom_classes.py:52`, umbra, 7.755

**Defensible.** It is the only subclass of `HelpFormatter` in the repository
and the session never opened that file, so "who extends the class you changed"
is a question a reviewer should ask and Umbra answered it correctly. But the
subclass overrides `write_heading` and nothing else, and the test around it
asserts on a styled heading. Nothing in this change can reach it. It takes the
top slot on a far-field multiplier of 1.5 awarded for sitting in `tests/`
rather than `src/`, which is a fact about directory layout, not about risk,
and that 1.5 is what puts it above the one node whose behaviour actually
changed. A reviewer loses fifteen seconds here. Right question, wrong answer,
top billing.

### 2. `test_wrap_text_visible_width`, `tests/test_formatting.py:487`, glance, 7.5

**Right, and the best thing in the report.** It is the only test in click that
calls `wrap_text` directly, and `wrap_text` is the function whose signature
and `TextWrapper` construction changed. If the `break_on_hyphens` plumbing had
been wrong, this is the test that would have said so. The `glance` tier is
also exactly right and non-obvious: the file was read, but with a range of
lines 505 to 604, and this test starts at 487, so it was in a file the session
opened and outside the part it saw. Selecting it as the sole probe was the
correct single choice.

### 3. `Command.format_usage`, `src/click/core.py:1163`, echo, 5.33

**Right node, wrong rank. This should have been first.** Its body is
`formatter.write_usage(ctx.command_path, " ".join(pieces))`. It is the only
call site in click of the method that changed, and every usage line click has
ever printed goes through it. It is third for two reasons, and both are
defects rather than judgements:

- It was demoted from umbra to **echo**, a 0.7 multiplier, because the string
  `src/click/core.py` appears in the session's own prose. It appears in a
  table comparing candidate repositories, written **before the repository was
  cloned**, in the sentence "dense intra-package call graph (`core.py` and
  `types.py` and `parser.py` and `decorators.py` and `termui.py`)". A
  filename typed while choosing between three projects downgraded eleven
  unexamined symbols in the winner. The packet states the reason plainly, "the
  session named `src/click/core.py` in its own words and never opened it",
  which is honest and still the wrong conclusion.
- It is labelled a **type consumer** rather than a direct caller, weight 2
  instead of 3, because Umbra never asked Graph about the method that changed.
  Section 6 has the mechanism. Asked directly, Graph answers
  `Command.format_usage CALLS depth 1`.

### 4. `Command.format_options`, `src/click/core.py:1300`, echo, 5.019

**Wrong.** It calls `formatter.write_dl(opts)` and never touches
`write_usage`. `write_dl` calls `wrap_text` with the default
`break_on_hyphens=True`, which this change deliberately left alone. There is
no input for which its output differs before and after the commit. It is in
the field for one reason only: its signature is
`(self, ctx: Context, formatter: HelpFormatter)`, a `PARAM_TYPE` edge from the
changed class. Ranking a node that cannot be affected above the public API
that renders the changed line is the ranker asserting something false.

### 5. `Command.format_arguments`, `src/click/core.py:1312`, echo, 4.651

**Wrong, for the same reason.** Also `write_dl`. And it shares its score of
4.651 with `format_commands`, `format_epilog`, `format_help`,
`format_help_text`, `make_formatter` and `Command.get_usage`, so the
ordering inside that block is a tie broken by path and name. `get_usage` is
the public entry point to the behaviour that changed and it sits at the
bottom of that tie; `Command.get_help` is below all of them at 4.2. **Within
`core.py` the ranking carries no information about which nodes the change can
reach.** It is ordering by dependent count, which measures how important a
symbol is in general, not how exposed it is to this diff.

### What the top five missed

`UsageError.show` at `src/click/exceptions.py:106` calls `self.ctx.get_usage()`
and prints the usage line on every parameter error in every click program. It
is a real behavioural dependent of this change and **it is not in the field at
all**, at any rank. `--depth 3` was tried and produced a byte-identical field:
the limit is not depth, it is that `self.ctx.get_usage()` is a method call on
an attribute and Graph resolves no edge for it. The README's "graph edges are
incomplete" is a one-line limitation on the fixture and a structural one on an
object-oriented codebase.

Also absent: all 46 assertions on `Usage:` across six test files. Not one of
them entered the field.

## 6. What broke

Five product failures and three environment or setup notes. None of them
crashed anything: `entire umbra` returned exit 0 on all five runs and never
panicked.

### F1. A changed method never binds to a symbol, so it is never traversed

`graph commit --json` named the changed method `HelpFormatter.write_usage`.
Umbra's `graph.Bind` looks it up with `f.Symbols[id].Name == name`
(`internal/graph/sources.go:287`). The snapshot record is:

```json
{"name": "write_usage", "qualified_name": "HelpFormatter.write_usage",
 "kind": "method", "file_path": "src/click/formatting.py", "start_line": 167}
```

`Name` is bare, the commit diff supplies the qualified form, the comparison
fails, `Source.Symbol` stays empty, and `analyze.go:117` skips the impact call
for any source with an empty symbol. The report still lists
`HelpFormatter.write_usage  body changed  src/click/formatting.py:167` with
`dependents 8`, which reads as though those eight were followed. They were
not. The word `qualified_name` appears nowhere in Umbra's Go source outside
test fixture data.

The eight were available for the asking:

```
entire graph impact --symbol write_usage --file src/click/formatting.py --line 167
  callers total 3
    Command.format_usage   src/click/core.py  CALLS  depth 1
    Command.get_usage      src/click/core.py  CALLS  depth 2
    Command.format_help    src/click/core.py  CALLS  depth 2
```

Real `CALLS` edges, correctly ranked by any reading. Instead the field was
built from the enclosing **class**, whose impact answer is
`callers: total 0` and eighteen type consumers.

**This affects every changed method in every object-oriented codebase.** The
fixture never showed it because `compute_total`, `handle_order`, `quote` and
`summarize` are all module-level functions, whose bare and qualified names are
identical.

### F2. The sweep reports zero leaks once more than sixteen tests fail

This is the serious one.

A mutation was planted in `HelpFormatter.write_usage` that upper-cases the
usage prefix. It breaks **55 tests** by pytest's count and **51** by
`graph verify`'s. Umbra's report:

```
probes  no test reaches the shadow
sweep   full suite  0 leaks
```

A clean, confident all-clear on a change that breaks fifty-five tests.

The cause was pinned rather than guessed. `graph verify` prints both a
`NEWLY FAILING (n): ...` line and a `VERDICT: REGRESSION in n tests: ...`
line when `n` is small, and **only the `VERDICT:` line when `n` is large**.
Measured on this repository with the same runner and worktrees, varying only
the number of failing ids:

| Newly failing | `NEWLY FAILING` line present |
|---|---|
| 3, 5, 8, 12, 16 | yes |
| 17, 18, 19, 47, 51 | **no** |

Umbra's `ParseVerdict` reads ids from `newlyFailingRE` and `newlyPassingRE`
only (`internal/graph/verify.go:38`). `execute.go:99` builds the changed set
from `v.NewlyFailing` and `v.NewlyPassing`. With neither line present both are
empty, so the leak list is empty and the count printed is zero. The `VERDICT:`
line, which carries the same ids, is captured as a display string and never
parsed. Nothing anywhere says the sweep could not read its own output.

**A known-positive confirms the mechanism.** A second mutation in
`write_heading` breaks 15 tests, one under the threshold. Same repository,
same runner, same code path:

```
probes  no test reaches the shadow
sweep   full suite  15 leaks
        tests/test_formatting.py::test_basic_functionality   test file not in the co-change set
        tests/test_custom_classes.py::test_context_formatter_class   reaches only through structure
        ... 13 more, each named with a reason
```

Fifteen leaks, all named, all with forensics. The machinery works perfectly.
It stops working, without saying so, at seventeen. The fixture's worst case is
five cracked probes, so this could not have appeared there.

This is the failure mode the README's limitations section names as the
project's own recurring sin, "a check that has never been observed to fail is
not yet a check", arriving in the check that audits all the others.

### F3. A module-granularity diff is reported as "no dependents"

A different one-character mutation, adding a trailing space inside an
f-string in `write_usage`, made `graph commit --json` answer at module
granularity:

```json
{"type": "body_changed", "kind": "module",
 "name": "src/click/formatting.py", "dependents_count": 0}
```

Umbra's report for that commit:

```
src/click/formatting.py  body changed  src/click/formatting.py:1
light     0 lit  0 penumbra  0 umbra  0 unknown   examined set unavailable
 no dependents were found for the changed symbols
probes  no test reaches the shadow
sweep   full suite  0 leaks
```

That commit breaks 51 tests. "No dependents were found for the changed
symbols" is a sentence about Graph's answer being unusable, printed in the
voice of a finding about the code.

The degradation is narrow and reproducible. Three control commits were made
against the same base: a one-line change in a top-level function body resolved
to `function wrap_text` with 6 dependents; a one-character change inside
another method resolved to the class and the method; a different line inside
`write_usage` itself resolved to `method HelpFormatter.write_usage` with 8
dependents. Only the trailing-whitespace-inside-a-string-literal case
degrades. Whatever the cause inside Graph, Umbra has no notion that a `module`
kind is a degraded answer and should be reported as one.

### F4. Selection reached no test on a real change

On both planted mutations, Umbra printed `probes  no test reaches the shadow`
and selected nothing. On the real commit it selected one test out of 2,059,
and that one arrived through `wrap_text`, a module-level function, not through
the method that changed.

The `TESTS` relation count for the whole repository is **18**, against 2,059
collected tests. Graph barely knows which tests exercise what in click, and
the paths that would substitute for that knowledge, `test -> CliRunner.invoke
-> Command.main -> ... -> format_usage -> write_usage`, run through dynamic
dispatch that produces no edges.

**Probe selection did not work on this repository.** It is worth being precise
about the consequence: on a 3 second suite it does not matter, because you run
everything. It would matter a great deal on a suite where you cannot.

### F5. A filename in prose demotes unexamined code

Covered in section 5. Eleven nodes moved from umbra to echo, a 0.7 multiplier,
because a filename was typed in a sentence written before the repository was
cloned. The report is honest about why, and the effect is still wrong: naming
a file while choosing a project is not attention paid to the code in it.

An agent in an ordinary session that says "I will need to check `core.py`" and
then does not check it produces exactly the same demotion, so this is not an
artifact of the import workaround.

### F6. Worktree isolation does not survive an editable install

Section 2. Worked around with a `PYTHONPATH` wrapper; the report says nothing
about whether isolation held.

### F7. `--depth 3` changed nothing

Identical field, identical thirteen shadowed nodes, identical scores. Umbra's
own BFS does use the flag, so the finding is that there were no further edges
to follow, not that the flag is ignored. A reviewer who reaches for `--depth 3`
because the field looks thin gets no signal that depth was not the problem.

### F8. `verify` and pytest disagree on the baseline count

`BASELINE RECORDED: ... (pytest; 1668 passing, 0 failing, exit 0)` against
pytest's own `2059 passed`. Consistent across runs. Not investigated, and it
does not affect the delta, but a baseline that undercounts by 391 tests is
worth knowing before anyone trusts the number.

### F9. Cross-repository path collision, an artifact of the setup

The imported transcript covers a session that also worked in the Umbra
repository. Umbra filters timeline paths against the target repository's file
list, and `README.md` exists in both, so `wc -l README.md` run against Umbra
marked click's `README.md` as `quoted`. This is a consequence of importing a
transcript from another repository, which is not normal usage. Recorded so it
is not mistaken for a real result.

## 7. What surprised me

**The shell blind spot went from a footnote to the dominant effect.** It is
already in the README, and I still did not expect 3 reads against 43 shell
commands, or 19 percent illumination on a change I understood completely.
Appending tests with a heredoc and patching a changelog with an inline Python
script are not unusual things for an agent to do; they are the obvious things
to do. The stated limitation is not an edge case, it is the common case.

**The safety net fails precisely when the selection is worst.** The sweep is
sold as the reason a thin selection is acceptable. A thin selection and a
large blast radius are the same event, and a large blast radius is exactly
what silences the sweep. The two failures are correlated in the worst possible
direction, and nothing in the design anticipated that because the fixture's
blast radius is five tests.

**Graph was better than Umbra's use of it.** Asked directly about
`write_usage`, Graph returned three correct `CALLS` callers, correctly ranked,
in three seconds. Umbra never asked. The best evidence in the system was one
string comparison away and the report instead described a `PARAM_TYPE` edge as
though it were the finding.

**The ranking was more defensible than I expected and its reasons were worse
than I expected.** Two of five defensible or right, and none of the five got
there by a chain of reasoning I would endorse. The top node won on a
directory-layout multiplier. The third node lost on a filename typed before
the repository existed. When a heuristic reaches a reasonable answer through
factors that are individually wrong, more test repositories will not tell you
that, only opening the source will.

**Nothing crashed.** Five runs, exit 0 every time, no panic, no hang, and
every degradation printed a note. The failure mode of this product is not
falling over. It is answering.

## 8. What this says about generalising

The parts that generalised: resolving a commit to a checkpoint, worktrees, the
transcript adapter, the classifier, the tier assignment, the scrubber, the
report renderers, the packet, exit codes, and the honesty of the notes. All of
that ran on an unfamiliar 28,000-line repository first time, and the packet's
prose explanations of why a node has the state it has were accurate every time
I checked one against the transcript. Performance is fine: 28 seconds, of
which 15 is a Graph index rebuilt five times, which is a caching problem and
not an architectural one.

The parts that did not generalise are the parts that touch the shape of real
code:

1. Changed methods do not bind, so a class-based codebase loses the strongest
   edges in the graph. **Fixture-invisible: everything in `fixtures/app` is a
   module-level function.**
2. The sweep goes blind above sixteen failures. **Fixture-invisible: the
   fixture's worst case is five.**
3. A module-granularity diff is reported as an absence of dependents rather
   than an absence of information.
4. Tests are two or more unresolvable hops from most production symbols, so
   probe selection selects almost nothing.
5. Ranking within a group of type consumers carries no information about
   whether the change can reach them.

Three of those five are not degradations under a real repository, they are
defects that a fixture built by the same author cannot express. That is the
honest summary of this experiment: **the fixture validated the pipeline and
could not validate the analysis.**

Whether the product generalises is not yet answered by this run, because F1
and F2 have to be dealt with before a second run means anything. F1 means the
central case, an agent changing a method, has never actually been exercised
end to end. F2 means the audit that would have told us so was reporting zero.
What can be said is narrower and still worth something: the machinery
generalises, the numbers on this run were mostly measuring the wrong edges,
and the ranking, given the wrong edges, was still right about one node in
five and defensible about a second.

## 9. Reproducing this

```sh
git clone https://github.com/pallets/click ~/umbra-experiment/click
cd ~/umbra-experiment/click && git checkout 6aabf09
python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -e . pytest
entire enable --agent claude-code && entire configure --skip-push-sessions
# make a change, commit it, then:
entire umbra <commit> --test "<runner> -v" --out ./out
```

The runner must be on `PATH` and must import the source from the worktree it
is standing in, not from an editable install. The wrapper used here:

```sh
#!/bin/sh
PYTHONPATH="$PWD/src${PYTHONPATH:+:$PYTHONPATH}"
export PYTHONPATH
exec /path/to/.venv/bin/python -m pytest "$@"
```

To reproduce F2 without any of the rest: record a baseline with
`entire graph verify --record-baseline`, then break seventeen or more tests
and adjudicate. `graph verify` reports the regression on its `VERDICT:` line
and prints no `NEWLY FAILING` line, and `entire umbra` reports zero leaks.

Tooling: Entire CLI 0.10.5, entire-graph
`v0.4.1-nightly.202609030616.ddcebd05`, Umbra at `7661eb2`, Python 3.14.4,
pytest 9.1.1, Linux.

Done. Report committed on branch `experiment/first-real-repo` as `917b3dd`; `go test ./...` green; your pending `site/` edits untouched.

**The answer is no, not yet.** Umbra ran clean on `pallets/click` (28k lines, 2,059 tests, 3s suite) and produced a confident report that was measuring the wrong edges.

**Three defects the fixture structurally cannot express:**

1. **A changed method never binds.** `graph commit` names it `HelpFormatter.write_usage`; the snapshot's `Name` field is the bare `write_usage`; `graph.Bind` compares on `Name`, so the match fails and `analyze.go:117` skips the impact query. The changed method's dependents were never traversed. Asked directly, Graph returns three correct `CALLS` callers in 3s. The fixture never showed this because all its changed symbols are module-level functions, where bare and qualified names are identical.

2. **The sweep goes blind above sixteen failures.** A planted mutation broke 55 tests; Umbra reported `sweep full suite 0 leaks`. `graph verify` prints `NEWLY FAILING (n):` at n≤16 and only the `VERDICT:` line at n≥17, and `ParseVerdict` reads ids from the former only. Pinned with a known-positive: 15 failures → 15 leaks named with forensics; 17+ → zero, silently. The audit that exists to cover a bad selection fails exactly when the selection is worst.

3. **A module-granularity diff is printed as "no dependents were found"** — an absence of information rendered in the voice of a finding, on a commit that broke 51 tests.

**Ranking, judged against source:** #2 right (the only direct `wrap_text` caller, correct `glance` tier), #1 defensible (the only `HelpFormatter` subclass, but reaches the top on a far-field multiplier for living in `tests/`), #3 right node wrong rank (`Command.format_usage` is the only call site of the changed method and should be first; it was demoted to `echo` because I typed `core.py` in prose *before cloning the repo*), #4 and #5 wrong (both call `write_dl`, unreachable from this change). `UsageError.show` and all 46 `Usage:` assertions were absent at any depth.

The machinery generalises. The analysis did not, and two of the three defects mean the central case — an agent changing a method — has never been exercised end to end.

You are in the Umbra repository. Read umbra/experiments/first-real-repo.md
(defect 2), then umbra/internal/graph/verify.go and the ParseVerdict path.

Fix: the sweep reports zero leaks when the suite has seventeen or more failures.
graph verify prints "NEWLY FAILING (n):" with ids only when n is at most 16, and
above that prints only the VERDICT line. ParseVerdict reads ids from the list
only, so above the threshold it sees none and the sweep reports a clean audit.
The audit fails exactly when the selection is worst.

Do this:
- Read the actual output shapes first, at 15, 17 and 55 failures, and record
  them verbatim in the commit message or NOTES. Do not guess the format.
- Prefer a JSON or machine-readable form of verify if one exists; check
  --help and capabilities before parsing human output. Say what you found.
- Make the count authoritative even when ids are unavailable. If verify reports
  a failure count but no ids, the sweep must report that it could not name the
  leaks and how many there are. It must never report zero leaks from a run whose
  ids it could not read. This is the same rule as the inconclusive-sweep fix
  already in the codebase; reuse that path rather than inventing a second one.
- Known-positive tests at 15, 17 and 55 failures, each proved to fail without
  the fix. The 15 case must still name leaks with forensics as it does today.

No em dashes. go test ./... green. Commit separately from any other work.

### F2. The sweep reports zero leaks once more than sixteen tests fail

This is the serious one.

A mutation was planted in `HelpFormatter.write_usage` that upper-cases the
usage prefix. It breaks **55 tests** by pytest's count and **51** by
`graph verify`'s. Umbra's report:

```
probes  no test reaches the shadow
sweep   full suite  0 leaks
```

A clean, confident all-clear on a change that breaks fifty-five tests.

The cause was pinned rather than guessed. `graph verify` prints both a
`NEWLY FAILING (n): ...` line and a `VERDICT: REGRESSION in n tests: ...`
line when `n` is small, and **only the `VERDICT:` line when `n` is large**.
Measured on this repository with the same runner and worktrees, varying only
the number of failing ids:

| Newly failing | `NEWLY FAILING` line present |
|---|---|
| 3, 5, 8, 12, 16 | yes |
| 17, 18, 19, 47, 51 | **no** |

Umbra's `ParseVerdict` reads ids from `newlyFailingRE` and `newlyPassingRE`
only (`internal/graph/verify.go:38`). `execute.go:99` builds the changed set
from `v.NewlyFailing` and `v.NewlyPassing`. With neither line present both are
empty, so the leak list is empty and the count printed is zero. The `VERDICT:`
line, which carries the same ids, is captured as a display string and never
parsed. Nothing anywhere says the sweep could not read its own output.

**A known-positive confirms the mechanism.** A second mutation in
`write_heading` breaks 15 tests, one under the threshold. Same repository,
same runner, same code path:

```
probes  no test reaches the shadow
sweep   full suite  15 leaks
        tests/test_formatting.py::test_basic_functionality   test file not in the co-change set
        tests/test_custom_classes.py::test_context_formatter_class   reaches only through structure
        ... 13 more, each named with a reason
```

Fifteen leaks, all named, all with forensics. The machinery works perfectly.
It stops working, without saying so, at seventeen. The fixture's worst case is
five cracked probes, so this could not have appeared there.

This is the failure mode the README's limitations section names as the
project's own recurring sin, "a check that has never been observed to fail is
not yet a check", arriving in the check that audits all the others.

### F3. A module-granularity diff is reported as "no dependents"

1	package graph
2	
3	import (
4		"context"
5		"regexp"
6		"sort"
7		"strings"
8		"time"
9	
10		"github.com/u7k4rs6/Umbra/umbra/internal/runner"
11	)
12	
13	// Verdict is what `graph verify` reported.
14	//
15	// The Step 0 probe pinned these shapes:
16	//
17	//	BASELINE RECORDED: /path (pytest; 14 passing, 0 failing, exit 0)
18	//	BASELINE RECORDED: /path (exit 0; output format not recognised, so the baseline is exit-code only)
19	//	NEWLY FAILING (3): tests/a.py::x, tests/a.py::y, tests/a.py::z
20	//	VERDICT: REGRESSION in 3 tests: ...
21	//	VERDICT: NO EFFECT ...
22	//
23	// The exit code is 0 even on a regression, so the verdict is read from the
24	// text and never from the status.
25	type Verdict struct {
26		NewlyFailing []string
27		NewlyPassing []string
28		PreExisting  []string
29		Line         string
30		// Degraded is set when verify could not parse per-test ids, which happens
31		// when the runner is not verbose.
32		Degraded bool
33		// TimedOut is set when the invocation hit its timeout.
34		TimedOut bool
35	}
36	
37	var (
38		newlyFailingRE = regexp.MustCompile(`(?m)^NEWLY FAILING\s*\(\d+\):\s*(.+)$`)
39		newlyPassingRE = regexp.MustCompile(`(?m)^NEWLY PASSING\s*\(\d+\):\s*(.+)$`)
40		preExistingRE  = regexp.MustCompile(`(?m)^PRE-EXISTING[^:]*:\s*(.+)$`)
41		verdictRE      = regexp.MustCompile(`(?m)^VERDICT:\s*(.+)$`)
42		degradedRE     = regexp.MustCompile(`(?i)output format not recognised|exit-code only`)
43	)
44	
45	// ParseVerdict reads the verify output.
46	func ParseVerdict(text string) Verdict {
47		var v Verdict
48		v.NewlyFailing = splitIDs(newlyFailingRE, text)
49		v.NewlyPassing = splitIDs(newlyPassingRE, text)
50		v.PreExisting = splitIDs(preExistingRE, text)
51		if m := verdictRE.FindStringSubmatch(text); m != nil {
52			v.Line = strings.TrimSpace(m[1])
53		}
54		v.Degraded = degradedRE.MatchString(text)
55		return v
56	}
57	
58	func splitIDs(re *regexp.Regexp, text string) []string {
59		m := re.FindStringSubmatch(text)
60		if m == nil {
61			return nil
62		}
63		var out []string
64		for _, part := range strings.Split(m[1], ",") {
65			part = strings.TrimSpace(part)
66			// verify caps its lists at twenty and appends a count.
67			if part == "" || strings.HasPrefix(part, "and ") {
68				continue
69			}
70			out = append(out, part)
71		}
72		sort.Strings(out)
73		return out
74	}
75	
76	// VerifyRequest is one pair of runs: record a baseline on the parent tree,
77	// then adjudicate the same command on the head tree.
78	type VerifyRequest struct {
79		BaseRepo     string
80		HeadRepo     string
81		Runner       []string
82		TestIDs      []string
83		BaselinePath string
84		Timeout      time.Duration
85	}
86	
87	// Command returns the argv Umbra passes to verify's --test flag.
88	//
89	// The runner prefix was split into argv once, at flag parsing, and the test
90	// ids are appended as separate elements. Umbra never joins them back into a
91	// shell string itself; verify takes a single --test string, so the pieces are
92	// joined here with spaces and every id has already been validated against
93	// ^[A-Za-z0-9_./:\[\]\-]+$, which cannot contain a space, a quote or a shell
94	// metacharacter.
95	func (r VerifyRequest) Command() string {
96		parts := append(append([]string(nil), r.Runner...), r.TestIDs...)
97		return strings.Join(parts, " ")
98	}
99	
100	// Verify runs the baseline and the adjudicated run.
101	//
102	// A missing base worktree, which happens for a root commit, means there is no
103	// baseline: the head run still happens and the verdict is a state rather than
104	// a delta. That is reported, not hidden.
105	func Verify(ctx context.Context, run runner.Runner, req VerifyRequest) (Verdict, []string, error) {
106		var commands []string
107		var baselineDegraded bool
108		cmd := req.Command()
109	
110		timeout := req.Timeout
111		if timeout <= 0 {
112			timeout = runner.VerifyTimeout
113		}
114	
115		if req.BaseRepo != "" {
116			args := []string{"graph", "verify", "--repo", req.BaseRepo, "--test", cmd, "--record-baseline", req.BaselinePath}
117			commands = append(commands, "entire "+strings.Join(args, " "))
118	
119			bctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, timeout)
120			stdout, _, _, err := run.Run(bctx, "entire", args, nil)
121			cancel()
122			if err != nil {
123				if bctx.Err() != nil {
124					return Verdict{TimedOut: true}, commands, nil
125				}
126				return Verdict{}, commands, err
127			}
128			// A baseline that could not name tests means the runner was not
129			// verbose. Carry that forward so the report can say so even when the
130			// head run happens to print a parseable line.
131			baselineDegraded = degradedRE.MatchString(string(stdout))
132		}
133	
134		args := []string{"graph", "verify", "--repo", req.HeadRepo, "--test", cmd}
135		if req.BaseRepo != "" {
136			args = append(args, "--pre-edit-baseline", req.BaselinePath)
137		} else {
138			args = append(args, "--record-baseline", req.BaselinePath+".head")
139		}
140		commands = append(commands, "entire "+strings.Join(args, " "))
141	
142		hctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, timeout)
143		defer cancel()
144		stdout, stderr, _, err := run.Run(hctx, "entire", args, nil)
145		if err != nil {
146			if hctx.Err() != nil {
147				return Verdict{TimedOut: true}, commands, nil
148			}
149			return Verdict{}, commands, err
150		}
151	
152		text := string(stdout)
153		if strings.TrimSpace(text) == "" {
154			text = string(stderr)
155		}
156		v := ParseVerdict(text)
157		v.Degraded = v.Degraded || baselineDegraded
158		return v, commands, nil
159	}

Run a test command and return an adjudicated verdict, not test output

Usage:
  entire graph verify --test "<cmd>" --repo . [--setup "<cmd>"] [--record-baseline path | --pre-edit-baseline path] [--max-bytes 2048]

verify runs your test command and reports WHICH TESTS CHANGED rather than what the runner printed: which newly pass, which newly fail, and which were ALREADY failing before the edit (labelled PRE-EXISTING). Raw runner output is never forwarded — ids are, text is not — and id lists cap at 20 with a count.

Record a baseline on the pristine tree first (--record-baseline), then pass that file as --pre-edit-baseline after editing. Without a baseline the verdict is a state rather than a delta, so a failure that predates the change cannot be labelled as one.

Parsers: pytest, jest/vitest, cargo test, go test, phpunit, rspec, minitest, maven/gradle surefire, ctest. An unrecognised format degrades to an exit-code-only verdict and says so.

Flags:
  --test <cmd>                 The test command to run (required)
  --repo <path>                Repository to run in (default: current repo)
  --setup <cmd>                Command run before the tests; its output never contributes test ids
  --record-baseline <path>     Write the pristine-tree result to this file instead of adjudicating
  --pre-edit-baseline <path>   Diff this run against a previously recorded baseline
  --max-bytes <n>              Cap the rendered verdict; the verdict clause always survives (default: 2048)

Examples:
  entire graph verify --repo . --test "pytest tests/test_parser.py" --record-baseline /tmp/base.json
  entire graph verify --repo . --test "pytest tests/test_parser.py" --pre-edit-baseline /tmp/base.json
